column2: The Introduction: on the merit of the science of history, the verification of its approaches, an allusion to the errors that befall historians, and mention of some of their causes

Know that the art of history is precious in its approach, rich in benefits and noble in its aim. For it informs us about the conditions of bygone nations in their character; of the prophets in their lives; of kings in their dynasties and their statecraft, so that the benefit of taking them as models is complete for anyone who seeks it in matters of religion and of this world. It therefore requires many sources, varied kinds of knowledge, good judgment and careful verification, which lead their possessor to the truth and turn him away from slips and errors. For when reports are relied on for mere transmission, and the principles of the normal course of things, the rules of statecraft, the nature of civilization and the conditions of human social organization are not applied to them, and the absent is not measured by what is observed, nor the present by what has gone, there may well be no safety in them from stumbling, a slip of the foot and straying from the highway of truth. Historians, Qurʾān commentators and leading transmitters have very often fallen into errors in stories and events, because they relied on mere transmission, whether lean or fat, and did not test them against their principles, nor measure them against their likes, nor probe them by the standard of philosophy, a grasp of the natures of created things, and the application of reasoning and insight to reports. So they strayed from the truth and wandered in the wilderness of delusion and error, especially in counting numbers of money and of armies when these come up in stories, for these are the likeliest place for falsehood and the mount of idle talk. They must be referred back to the principles and set against the rules.

An example is what al-Masʿūdī and many historians relate about the armies of the Children of Israel: that Moses, peace be upon him, counted them in the wilderness, after he had accepted only those able to bear arms, from the age of twenty upward, and they were 600,000 or more. In this they are heedless of gauging Egypt and Syria and whether their extent could hold such a number of troops. For every kingdom has a share of garrison that it has room for and can provide for, and is too narrow for any more; this is attested by well-known customs and familiar conditions. Moreover, it is unlikely that armies reaching such a number could advance on one another or fight, because the expanse of the earth is too narrow for them, and because, once drawn up in line, their extent would be beyond the range of sight, two or three times over or more. How, then, could these two parties fight, or the victory of one line be achieved while some of its flanks have no awareness of the other flank? The present bears witness to this, for the past resembles the future more than water resembles water.

The royal authority and dynasty of the Persians were far greater than the royal authority of the Children of Israel. Proof of this is Nebuchadnezzar’s (Bukhtnaṣṣar) victory over the Israelites, his swallowing up of their land and taking control of their affairs, and his destruction of Jerusalem, the capital of their religious community and of their sovereignty, although he was one of the governors of the Persian kingdom; it is said that he was marzbān of the western frontier of Persia. Their kingdoms in the two Iraqs, Khurāsān, Transoxania and al-Abwāb were far wider than those of the Children of Israel, and yet the Persian armies never reached such a number, nor anything near it. The largest of their forces, at al-Qādisiyya, was 120,000, every one of them with a following, according to what Sayf reported; he said that with their followers they were more than 200,000. And according to ʿĀʾisha and al-Zuhrī, the forces of Rustam, against whom Saʿd advanced at al-Qādisiyya, were only 60,000, every one of them with a following. Further, had the Children of Israel reached such a number, the compass of their royal authority would have been wide and the range of their dynasty broad, for the provinces and kingdoms within dynasties are in proportion to the garrison and the tribal group that sustain them, in their fewness and their multitude, as we shall explain in the chapter on kingdoms in Book One. Yet the kingdoms of these people extended no further than the Jordan and Palestine in Syria, and the land of Yathrib and Khaybar in the Hijaz, as is well known.

Furthermore, between Moses and Israel there are only four forefathers, as the verifiers state. He is Moses son of ʿImrān son of Yaṣhar son of Qāhat (with a fatḥa or a kasra on the hāʾ) son of Lāwī (with a kasra or a fatḥa on the wāw) son of Jacob, who is Israel of God. So his genealogy is given in the Torah. As for the time between them, according to what al-Masʿūdī relates, he said: Israel entered Egypt with his sons, the Tribes, and their children, when they came to Joseph, seventy persons, and their stay in Egypt, until they went out with Moses, peace be upon him, to the wilderness, was 220 years, during which the Coptic kings, the pharaohs, ruled over them in turn. It is unlikely that offspring could branch out in four generations to such a number. And if they claim that the number of those armies was reached only in the time of Solomon and after him, that too is unlikely, for between Solomon and Israel there are only eleven forefathers. He is Solomon son of David son of Yashā son of ʿŪfīdh (also said to be son of ʿŪfidh) son of Bāʿiz (also said: Būʿiz) son of Salmūn son of Naḥshūn son of ʿAmīnūdhab (also said: Ḥamīnādhāb) son of Ram son of Ḥaṣrūn (also said: Ḥasrūn) son of Bāris (also said: Bibaras) son of Judah son of Jacob. And offspring cannot branch out within eleven generations to such a number as they claimed; at most to hundreds and thousands, which may be, but that it should go beyond them to the higher orders of numbers is unlikely. Judge this by what is present and observed and by what is recent and well known, and you will find their claim false and their report untrue.

What is established in Israelite lore is that Solomon’s troops were only 12,000, and that his prized horses numbered 1,400, tethered at his gates. This is the sound part of their reports, and no attention is paid to the fables of their common people. In the days of Solomon (peace be upon him) and in his reign, their dynasty was at its height and their kingdom at its widest. Now we find that people in general of this age, when they speak at length about the armies of the dynasties of their own time or close to it, or discuss reports about the armies of the Muslims or the Christians, or set about counting the money from tax revenues and the sultan’s land tax, the expenditures of the luxurious, and the wares of the wealthy and well-off, go deep into numbers, exceed the limits of custom, and yield to the whisperings of the love of the extraordinary. Yet when the officials in charge of the registers are questioned about their armies, and the circumstances of the wealthy are investigated as to their wares and revenues, and the habits of the luxurious are clarified as to their expenditures, you will not find a tenth of what they count. This is only because the soul is passionately fond of the strange, the tongue oversteps with ease, and the one who should check and criticize is heedless, so that he does not call himself to account for mistake or intent, nor demand of himself moderation or fairness in a report, nor bring it back to investigation and scrutiny; he lets loose his reins and lets his tongue graze in the pastures of falsehood, takes the signs of God in mockery, and buys idle talk to lead astray from the path of God. And that, as a losing bargain, is enough for you.

Among the historians’ weak reports is what they all relate in the reports of the Tubbaʿs, kings of Yemen and the Arabian Peninsula: that they used to raid from their villages in Yemen to Ifrīqiya and the Berbers in the lands of the Maghrib; that Afrīqish son of Qays son of Ṣayfī, one of the greatest of their early kings, who lived in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, or a little before, raided Ifrīqiya and inflicted heavy slaughter on the Berbers; that it was he who gave them this name, when he heard their jabber and said, “What is this barbara?”, so that the name was taken from him and they have been called by it ever since; and that when he withdrew from the Maghrib he left behind there tribes of Ḥimyar, who settled there and mixed with its people, among them Ṣanhāja and Kutāma. On this basis al-Ṭabarī, al-Jurjānī, al-Masʿūdī, Ibn al-Kalbī and al-Bīlī held that Ṣanhāja and Kutāma are of Ḥimyar, but the genealogists of the Berbers reject this, and theirs is the sound view. Al-Masʿūdī also mentions that Dhū al-Adhʿār, one of their kings before Afrīqish, who lived in the time of Solomon (peace be upon him), raided the Maghrib and subdued it, and he mentions the same of Yāsir, his son after him, and that he reached the Valley of Sand in the lands of the Maghrib and found no way through because of the quantity of sand, and turned back. They say likewise of the later Tubbaʿ, Asʿad Abū Karib, who lived in the time of Yastāsif, one of the Kayanid kings of Persia, that he ruled Mosul and Azerbaijan and met the Turks and defeated them and inflicted heavy slaughter, then raided them a second and a third time in the same way; and that after that he sent three of his sons to raid, to the land of Persia, to the land of Sogdiana, in the lands of the Turkish nations beyond the River, and to the land of the Rūm. The first took the lands as far as Samarkand and crossed the wasteland to China, and found that his brother, the second, who had raided as far as Samarkand, had reached China before him; the two of them inflicted heavy slaughter in the land of China and returned together with the spoils, leaving in China tribes of Ḥimyar, who are there to this day. The third reached Constantinople, which he razed, and subdued the land of the Rūm, and returned.

These reports are all far from sound, deeply rooted in delusion and error, and more like invented tales. The reason is that the Tubbaʿs’ royal authority was only in the Arabian Peninsula, and their seat and throne were at Sanaa in Yemen. The Arabian Peninsula is surrounded by sea on three sides: the Indian Ocean on the south; the Persian Gulf, which descends from it to Basra, on the east; and the Sea of Suez (the Red Sea), which descends from it to Suez, one of the districts of Egypt, on the west, as you see on the geographical map. So those traveling from Yemen to the Maghrib find no route except by way of Suez, and the passage there, between the Sea of Suez and the Syrian Sea (the Mediterranean), is about two stages or less. It is unlikely that a great king with ample armies would go through this passage without it becoming one of his own districts. This is impossible in the normal course of things. In those districts there were the Amalekites, and the Canaanites in Syria and the Copts in Egypt; later the Amalekites ruled Egypt and the Children of Israel ruled Syria. It has never been reported that the Tubbaʿs fought any of these nations or ruled any of those districts. Furthermore, the distance from the sea to the Maghrib is great and the provisions and fodder needed for armies are many. If they marched outside their own districts, they would need to plunder crops and livestock and to plunder the lands they passed through, and normally that does not suffice for provisions and fodder; and if they carried what they needed from their own districts, their mounts could not manage to transport it. So they must pass all along their route through districts they had already taken possession of

and subdued, so that their supplies would come from them. And if we say that those armies pass through these nations without provoking them and obtain their supplies by peaceful dealing, that is still more unlikely and even more impossible. This shows that these reports are weak or invented. As for the Valley of Sand, which defeats the traveler, its mention has never been heard in the Maghrib, despite the multitude of those who travel there and of those who follow its routes, whether riders or villagers, in every age and every region; and, being as strange as they said, the motives to report it would be abundant. As for their raiding the lands of the East and the land of the Turks, although the route is wider than the passages of Suez, the distance here is greater, and the nations of Persia and the Rūm lie across it before the Turks. It has never been reported that the Tubbaʿs ruled the land of Persia or the land of the Rūm. They only fought the Persians on the borders of the land of Iraq, between al-Baḥrayn and al-Ḥīra, and in al-Jazīra between the Tigris and the Euphrates and the districts between them. That occurred between Dhū al-Adhʿār of the Tubbaʿs and Kaykāwus, one of the Kayanid kings, and between the younger Tubbaʿ Abū Karib and Yastāsif, who was also one of them, and with the Party Kings after the Kayanids and the Sasanians after them. [As for] crossing the land of

Persia in raiding to the land of the Turks and Tibet, that is impossible in the normal course of things, because of the nations lying in the way and the need for provisions and fodder, together with the great distance, as has been said. So the reports about this are weak and flawed; and even if they were soundly transmitted, that would impugn them, how much more when they were not transmitted by any sound route. As for Ibn Isḥāq’s statement in his report about Yathrib, the Aws and the Khazraj, that the later Tubbaʿ marched to the East, it is to be taken as referring to Iraq and the land of Persia; as for the land of the Turks and Tibet, it is not sound that they raided there in any way, for the reasons established. So do not trust what is thrown to you of this, but examine reports and set them against the sound rules, and you will be able to sift them out in the best way. And God is the guide to what is right.

More remote than that, and more deeply rooted in delusion, is what the Qurʾān commentators pass on in their commentary on the sura “By the Dawn” (al-Fajr), on the words of God the Exalted: “Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the pillars?” (89: 6–7). They make the word Iram the name of a city described as having pillars, that is, columns, and they relate that ʿĀd son of ʿAwṣ son of Iram had two sons, Shadīd and Shaddād, who ruled after him; Shadīd died and the kingship passed to Shaddād alone, and their kings submitted to him. He heard a description of Paradise and said, “I shall build the like of it.” So he built the city of Iram in the deserts of Aden over 300 years, his age being 900 years. It was a great city, its palaces of gold and its columns of peridot and ruby, and in it were all kinds of trees and running rivers. When its building was complete, he set out for it with the people of his kingdom, and when they were a day and a night’s journey from it, God sent a cry upon them from heaven, and they all perished. This is recorded by al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Zamakhsharī and other commentators. They also relate on the authority of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qilāba, one of the Companions, that he went out looking for camels of his and came upon the city and carried off from it what he could; his report reached Muʿāwiya, who had him brought, and he told him. Muʿāwiya sought out Kaʿb al-Aḥbār and asked him about it, and he said, “It is Iram of the pillars, and a man of the Muslims will enter it, ruddy, fair-haired and short, with a mole on his eyebrow and a mole on his neck, who will go out looking for camels of his.” Then he turned, saw Ibn Qilāba, and said, “By God, this is that man.”

No report of this city has been heard from that day to this in any part of the earth. The deserts of Aden in which they claim it was built are in the middle of Yemen, whose civilization has been continuous, and guides recount its routes from every direction; yet no report of this city has been transmitted, and none of the chroniclers or the nations has mentioned it. If they had said that it had been effaced along with the monuments that were effaced, that would have been more plausible, but the apparent sense of their words is that it exists. Some of them say it is Damascus, on the ground that the people of ʿĀd ruled it, and the raving of some of them goes so far as to say that it is hidden and can only be found by people of spiritual exercise and magic. All of these are claims more like fables. What led the commentators to this was what the craft of grammatical analysis requires about the words “of the pillars”: that they are a description of Iram. They took “pillars” to mean columns, so it had to be a building. This was strengthened for them by Ibn al-Zubayr’s reading ʿĀd Iram, in the construct state without nunation. Then they came upon those stories, which are more like invented tales, nearer to falsehood, transmitted among the laughable anecdotes. Otherwise, ʿimād means the poles of tents, indeed of pavilions; and if columns are meant by it, there is nothing strange in describing them as people of building and columns in general, because of their well-known strength, not as a particular building in a specific city or elsewhere. And if it is put in construct, as in Ibn al-Zubayr’s reading, then it is by annexing the subdivision to the tribe, as you say Quraysh of Kināna, Ilyās of Muḍar, Rabīʿa of Nizār. What necessity is there for this remote interpretation, contrived in order to justify such feeble stories, of the like of which the Book of God is to be held free, because of their distance from soundness?

Among the historians’ flawed stories is what they all relate about the reason for al-Rashīd’s disgracing of the Barmakids: the story of his sister al-ʿAbbāsa with Jaʿfar ibn Yaḥyā ibn Khālid, his client. They say that, because of his fondness for the place they held in his wine-drinking with them, he allowed them to conclude a marriage contract but not to be alone together, out of eagerness to have them together in his assembly; that al-ʿAbbāsa used a ruse on [Jaʿfar] to be alone with him, because of the passion for his love that had seized her, until he lay with her (they claim, in a state of drunkenness) and she conceived; and that this was reported to al-Rashīd and he became enraged. How far that is from the standing of al-ʿAbbāsa in her religion, her parents and her dignity! She was a descendant of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, with only four men between her and him, who were the nobles of the religion and the great men of the community after him. For al-ʿAbbāsa was the daughter of Muḥammad al-Mahdī son of ʿAbd Allāh Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr son of Muḥammad al-Sajjād son of ʿAlī, Father of the Caliphs, son of ʿAbd Allāh, the interpreter of the Qurʾān, son of al-ʿAbbās, uncle of the Prophet (God bless him and grant him peace) — the daughter of a caliph and sister of a caliph, surrounded on all sides by mighty royal authority and prophetic caliphate, by companionship with the Messenger and by his uncles, by the establishment of the religion, the light of revelation and the place of the angels’ descent; close in time to the Arab Bedouin life and the simplicity of religion, far from the customs of luxury and the pastures of vice. Where, then, are guardedness and chastity to be sought if they are gone from her, or where are purity and intelligence to be found if they are lost from her house? Or how could she join her lineage to Jaʿfar ibn Yaḥyā

and sully her Arab nobility with a client from among the clients of the non-Arabs, whether by the ownership of his grandfather, one of the Persians, or by the clientage of her grandfather, one of the Messenger’s uncles and of the nobles of Quraysh? The most that can be said is that their dynasty took him and his father by the arm, drew them to itself and raised them to the ranks of the nobles. And how could it be proper for al-Rashīd, with his lofty ambition and the greatness of his forefathers, to ally himself by marriage with the clients of the non-Arabs? If one who reflects on this were to look at it as a fair-minded man would, and compare al-ʿAbbāsa with the daughter of a king from among the great kings of her time, he would think it beneath her to be given to such a man, a client of the clients of her own dynasty and under the authority of her own people; he would find it abhorrent and persist in calling it a lie. And how far above other people stand the rank of al-ʿAbbāsa and al-Rashīd!

What brought the Barmakids down was only their taking sole control of the dynasty and their withholding of the tax revenues, so that al-Rashīd would ask for a small sum of money and it would not reach him. They overpowered him in his affairs and shared with him in his sovereignty, and he had no freedom of action, with them, in the affairs of his kingship. So their influence grew great and their renown spread far; they filled the ranks and offices of the dynasty with chiefs from among their sons and their protégés and took them over to the exclusion of everyone else: the vizierate, secretaryship, military command, chamberlainship, sword and pen. It is said that in al-Rashīd’s court there were twenty-five chiefs from among the sons of Yaḥyā ibn Khālid, men of the sword and men of the pen, who jostled the people of the dynasty with their shoulders for these offices and pushed them away from them with the palms of their hands, by reason of their father Yaḥyā’s position in the guardianship of Hārūn, as heir apparent and as caliph, until he grew up in his lap and was reared from his nest; Yaḥyā gained mastery over his affairs, and Hārūn used to call him “my father.” So the sultan’s favor turned toward them, their assurance with him grew great, and their prestige widened among them; faces turned toward them, necks bowed to them, hopes were confined to them, and from the farthest borders the gifts of kings and the presents of emirs made their way to them, and tax revenues seeped into their treasuries by way of ingratiation and courting favor,

and they lavished gifts upon the partisans and the great men of the kin, ringed them with favors, provided for the penniless of noble houses, ransomed captives, and were praised as their own caliph was not praised; they raised high the prizes and gifts for those who sought their bounty, and took possession of villages and estates in the outlying districts and the cities of all the realms, until they vexed the entourage, filled the inner circle with rancor, and choked those in office. So the faces of rivalry and envy were unmasked toward them, and the scorpions of denunciation crept toward their soft couch in the dynasty; even the Banū Qaḥṭaba, Jaʿfar’s maternal uncles, were among the foremost of those who intrigued against them. The sympathies of kinship did not soften them, because of the envy settled in their souls, and the ties of relationship did not restrain them. Along with that, in their master there arose the first stirrings of jealousy, of disdain at being kept under tutelage, and of pride, and the rancors that were aroused in him by them came from petty acts of presumption. Their persistence in this conduct led on to grave acts of defiance, such as their handling of Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, brother of Muḥammad al-Mahdī, nicknamed al-Nafs al-Zakiyya, who rose against al-Manṣūr. This Yaḥyā is the one whom al-Faḍl ibn Yaḥyā brought down from the land of the Daylam on a guarantee of safety from al-Rashīd in his own hand, and he offered them 1,000,000 dirhams for him, as al-Ṭabarī reports. Al-Rashīd handed him over to Jaʿfar and placed his detention in his house and under his supervision. He kept him for a time; then his presumption moved him to set him free and, acting on his own, to undo his bonds, out of respect, as he claimed, for the sanctity of the blood of the Prophet’s household, and in presumption toward the sultan in his ruling.

And al-Rashīd asked him about [Yaḥyā] when it was reported to him; [Jaʿfar] understood and said, “I released him.” Al-Rashīd showed him an appearance of approval but kept it secret within himself, and so Jaʿfar opened the way against himself and his people until their throne was toppled, their sky was cast down upon them, and the earth swallowed them and their houses, and their days passed as a precedent and an example for those who came after. Whoever reflects on their reports and traces the history of the dynasty and of them will find that effect certain and its causes prepared. See what Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih relates of al-Rashīd’s discussion with the uncle of his grandfather, Dāwūd ibn ʿAlī, about the affair of their disgrace, and what he mentions in the chapter on poets in the book al-ʿIqd (“The Necklace”) about al-Aṣmaʿī’s conversation with al-Rashīd and with al-Faḍl ibn Yaḥyā during their evening talks, and you will understand that what killed them was only jealousy and rivalry over sole control, on the part of the caliph and those below him. The same is true of what their enemies in the entourage contrived, in the verse they slipped to the singers as a ruse to have the caliph hear it and arouse his resentments against them, namely:
Would that Hind would fulfill for us what she promises ... and heal our souls of what we feel / and take sole control just once ... the helpless one is only he who does not take sole control

And when al-Rashīd heard it he said, “Yes, by God, I am helpless,” until, with things like these, they roused his hidden jealousy and unleashed upon them the force of his vengeance. We seek refuge in God from being overcome by men and from a bad state.

As for what the story embellishes about al-Rashīd’s drinking wine and his drunkenness joining the drunkenness of his drinking companions, God forbid! We know of no evil in him. How far this is from the state of al-Rashīd: his performance of what the station of the caliphate requires of religion and justice; the company of scholars and saints that he kept; his conversations with al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ, Ibn al-Sammāk and al-ʿUmarī; his correspondence with Sufyān al-Thawrī; his weeping at their admonitions; his supplication at Mecca during his circumambulation; and the devotion he practiced, his care to observe the times of the prayers, and his attending the dawn prayer at the start of its time. Al-Ṭabarī and others report that he used to pray 100 supererogatory rakʿas every day, that he went on campaign one year and on pilgrimage the next, and that he rebuked Ibn Abī Maryam, his jester at his evening talks, when the jester made a jibe at him about prayer in the same vein: on hearing him recite “And why should I not worship Him who created me?” (36: 22), he said, “By God, I do not know why!”

So al-Rashīd could not help laughing; then he turned to him angrily and said, “Ibn Abī Maryam, in the prayer too? Beware, beware of the Qurʾān and religion; beyond those two, you may do as you please.” Moreover, he held a standing in knowledge and simplicity, owing to his closeness in time to his predecessors who followed that way, and there was no long time between him and his grandfather Abū Jaʿfar; he survived him only as a boy. Abū Jaʿfar held a standing in knowledge and religion before the caliphate and after it, and he is the one who said to Mālik, when he urged him to compose al-Muwaṭṭaʾ (“The Well-Trodden Path”), “Abū ʿAbd Allāh, there is no one left on the face of the earth more learned than I and you, and the caliphate has kept me occupied; so you set down for the people a book from which they can benefit, in which you avoid the concessions of Ibn ʿAbbās and the rigors of Ibn ʿUmar, and smooth the way for the people thoroughly.” Mālik said, “By God, he taught me composition that day.” And his son al-Mahdī, the father of this al-Rashīd, came upon him being scrupulous about clothing his household with new garments from the public treasury; al-Mahdī went in to see him one day while he was in his assembly, dealing directly with the tailors over patching the worn-out clothes of his household, and al-Mahdī found that distasteful and said, “Commander of the Faithful, I take upon myself the clothing of these dependents this year, from my allowance.” He said to him, “You may.” And he did not stop him from it, nor did he permit spending on it from the Muslims’ funds

So how would it befit al-Rashīd, given how close in time he was to this caliph and to his father, and given what he was brought up on of such ways in his family and the adoption of them as character, to drink wine habitually or to do so openly? The condition of the nobles of the pre-Islamic Arabs in avoiding wine was well known; the vine was not their tree, and drinking it was a disgrace among many of them. And al-Rashīd and his forefathers were at the very height of avoiding blameworthy things in their religion and their worldly affairs, and of taking on praiseworthy traits, qualities of perfection and Arab inclinations. See what al-Ṭabarī and al-Masʿūdī relate in the story of the physician Jibrīl ibn Bukhtīshūʿ, when fish was brought to al-Rashīd at his table and Jibrīl kept him from it, then ordered the steward of the table to carry it to his house; al-Rashīd noticed and grew suspicious of him, and secretly sent a servant until he saw him eating it. So Ibn Bukhtīshūʿ prepared, as an excuse, three pieces of fish in three cups: he mixed one with meat prepared with spices, vegetables, cold relishes and sweets, poured iced water over the second, and neat wine over the third. And he said of the first and the second, “This is the food of the Commander of the Faithful, whether the fish is mixed with other things or not,” and said of the third, “This is the food of Ibn Bukhtīshūʿ,”

and handed them to the steward of the table, so that when al-Rashīd became aware and summoned him to reproach him, he produced the three cups. He found the one with wine mixed up, dissolved and crumbled, and found the other two spoiled and their smell changed; so that was an excuse for him. It became clear from this that al-Rashīd’s state in avoiding wine was known among his entourage and the people of his table. It is established of him that he ordered Abū Nuwās imprisoned when it reached him how deeply he was absorbed in drinking, until he repented and gave it up. Al-Rashīd drank only date nabīdh, following the school of the people of Iraq, whose legal rulings on it are well known; as for neat wine, there is no way to accuse him of it, nor to accept without scrutiny the weak reports about it. The man was not one to commit a prohibited act that is among the greatest of the major sins in the view of the people of the faith. Indeed, all those people stood apart from indulging in extravagance and luxury in their clothing, their adornment and everything else they used, because of the roughness of Bedouin life and the simplicity of religion that they had not yet left. What do you think, then, of what passes from the permitted to the forbidden and from the lawful to the prohibited? The historians al-Ṭabarī, al-Masʿūdī and others agree that all the earlier caliphs of the Umayyads and the Abbasids rode with only a light ornament of silver on belts, swords, bridles and saddles, and that the first caliph to introduce riding with ornament of gold was al-Muʿtazz ibn al-Mutawakkil, the eighth caliph after al-Rashīd. Such was their state in their clothing too; what do you think, then, of their drinks?

And this becomes clear more fully than from what has been said once you grasp the nature of the dynasty in its beginning, in its Bedouin life and its freshness, as we shall explain in the questions of Book One, God willing. And God is the guide to what is right. Similar to this, or close to it, is what they all relate about Yaḥyā ibn Aktham, al-Maʾmūn’s judge and companion: that he drank wine, and that he got drunk one night along with his fellow drinkers and was buried in fragrant herbs until he came to; and they recite, in his voice:

My lord, and prince of all the people ... he who was pouring me drink has been unjust in his judgment / I was heedless of the cupbearer, and he made me ... as you see me, robbed of reason and religion

The case of Ibn Aktham and al-Maʾmūn in this is that of al-Rashīd: their drink was only nabīdh, which was not forbidden to them; as for drunkenness, it was not their way. His companionship with al-Maʾmūn was only a bond of friendship in religion, and it is established that he slept with him in the same room; and it is reported among al-Maʾmūn’s virtues and good companionship that he woke one night thirsty and got up and groped about looking for the vessel, for fear of waking Yaḥyā ibn Aktham; and it is established that the two of them prayed the dawn prayer together. How far is this from habitual drinking! Moreover, Yaḥyā ibn Aktham was among the elite of the people of hadith: the imam Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and Ismāʿīl the judge praised him, al-Tirmidhī transmitted on his authority in his book al-Jāmiʿ (“The Compendium”), and al-Muzanī the ḥāfiẓ mentions that al-Bukhārī transmitted from him outside al-Jāmiʿ; so to impugn him is to impugn all of them. Likewise what the libertines brand him with, a leaning toward boys, is slander against God and a lie against the scholars, and they rely in this on the weak reports of storytellers, which may be fabrications of his enemies, for he was envied for his perfection and his intimacy with the sultan, and his standing in knowledge and religion was too high for any such thing. When what people charge him with was mentioned to Ibn Ḥanbal, he said, “Glory be to God, glory be to God! Who says this?”

And he denied it most emphatically. And Ismāʿīl the judge praised him; when it was said to him, “What used to be said about him?” he said, “God forbid that the probity of a man like him be undone by the lies of a transgressor and an envious man.” He also said, “Yaḥyā ibn Aktham is too innocent before God for there to be in him any of what he was accused of regarding boys. I used to learn his inner thoughts and found him greatly in fear of God; but there was in him some playfulness and a good nature, so he was accused of what he was accused of.” Ibn Ḥibbān, in al-Thiqāt (“The Reliable Transmitters”), [lists him] and said, “Do not occupy yourself with what is related about him, for most of it is not authentic from him.” Among stories like these is what Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih, author of al-ʿIqd, relates in the story of the basket, as the reason for al-Maʾmūn’s marrying into the family of al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl through his daughter Būrān: that one night, in his wandering through the lanes of Baghdad, he came upon a basket let down from one of the roofs by hooks and cords of tightly twisted silk. He got into it and took hold of the hooks; they shook, and it carried him upward to a room of such and such a description, and [Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih] described the adornment of its furnishings, the arrangement of its structures and the beauty of its appearance, such as halts the eye and captivates the soul; and that a woman came out to him from between the curtains in that room, radiant in beauty, bewitching in her charms, and greeted him and invited him to drink with her

and he went on drinking with her until morning, and returned to his companions, who were waiting for him where they were, she having so captivated him with love that it moved him to seek marriage with her father. And how far is all this from al-Maʾmūn’s known state in his religion and his knowledge, his following the practices of the rightly guided caliphs among his forefathers, and his taking up the ways of the four caliphs, the pillars of the faith, his disputations with scholars, and his keeping of the bounds of God the Exalted in his prayers and judgments! How could the ways of the dissolute and reckless be authentic of him: wandering at night, calling at houses, and frequenting evening gatherings, the way of the lovers among the Bedouin Arabs? And how far is that from the station of the daughter of al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl and her nobility, and the guardedness and chastity at her father’s house! Stories like these are many and well known in the books of the historians. What prompts their invention and their telling is absorption in forbidden pleasures and the tearing of the veils of secluded women; and they excuse themselves by following those men’s example in what they do in obedience to their pleasures. That is why you see them so often devoted to reports of this kind and digging them out when they leaf through the pages of the registers. Had they followed those men in their other conditions and in the attributes of perfection that befit them and are famed of them, it would have been better for them, if they only knew.

I once rebuked one of the emirs, among the sons of kings, for his keenness to learn singing and his passion for stringed instruments, and I said to him, “This is not your business and does not befit your station.” He said to me, “Do you not see how Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mahdī was the master of this craft and the chief of the singers in his time?” I said to him, “Glory be to God! Why did you not follow his father or his brother? Do you not see how that kept Ibrāhīm back from their stations?” He turned a deaf ear to my rebuke and turned away. And “God guides whom He wills” (2: 213).

Among the weak reports is what many historians and men of established reliability hold concerning the ʿUbaydids, the caliphs of the Shīʿa in Qayrawān and Cairo: their denial that they belong to the Prophet’s family, God’s blessings be upon them, and their attack on their descent from Ismāʿīl the imam, son of Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq. They rely in this on reports fabricated for the weak Abbasid caliphs, to curry favor with them by disparaging whoever opposed them and by making an art of gloating over their enemy, as some of these reports are mentioned in the reports about them. And they fail to notice the evidence of events and the indications of conditions that required the opposite of this: the belying of their claim and the refutation of them.

They agree, in what they say about the beginning of the Shīʿite dynasty, that when Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Muḥtasib preached among the Kutāma for the one approved from the family of Muḥammad (al-riḍā), and word of him spread and it became known that he was hovering around ʿUbayd Allāh al-Mahdī and his son Abū al-Qāsim, the two feared for themselves and fled from the East, the seat of the caliphate, and passed through Egypt; that they left Alexandria in the dress of merchants and word of them reached ʿĪsā al-Nūshārī, governor of Egypt and Alexandria, who dispatched horsemen in search of them; and that when they were overtaken, their condition remained hidden from their pursuer by the garb and dress in which they had disguised themselves, so they escaped to the Maghrib. And that al-Muʿtaḍid sent word to the Aghlabids, emirs of Ifrīqiya at Qayrawān, and to the Banū Midrār, emirs of Sijilmāsa, to close off every horizon to them and to set spies in search of them; and Alīshaʿ, lord of Sijilmāsa, of the family of Midrār, came upon their hidden place in his city and detained them, to please the caliph.

This was before the Shīʿa prevailed over the Aghlabids at Qayrawān. Then after that came what came: the appearance of their mission in the Maghrib and Ifrīqiya, then in Yemen, then in Alexandria, then in Egypt, Syria and the Hijaz; and they shared the realms of Islam with the Abbasids half and half, like the two halves of a split palm-fiber, and they almost entered upon them in their homelands and displaced them from their rule. Indeed, the emir al-Basāsīrī, one of the clients of the Daylam who had gained mastery over the Abbasid caliphs, proclaimed their mission in Baghdad and its Iraq, in a quarrel that arose between him and the non-Arab emirs, and the khuṭba was given for them from its pulpits for a full year. The Abbasids kept choking on their standing and their dynasty, while the Umayyad kings across the sea cried out woe and war on account of them. How could all this happen for a false claimant to a lineage, who lies in laying claim to the cause? Consider the case of the Qarmaṭī, since he was a false claimant in his descent: how his mission dissolved, his followers dispersed, their malice and deceit were quickly exposed, their end was bad, and they tasted the evil consequence of their affair. Had the case of the ʿUbaydids been like that, it would have been known, even after a delay:
